Area.evidence_source: Risk: "The developmental history of the deceased revealed how negative experiences during their upbringing may have predisposed these men to develop maladaptive perfectionism as adults." [page/13/Text/6], "Maladaptive perfectionism seems to be related to an unsolved dependency of being recognized, especially by fathers (or father figures) who neglected and/or rejected the deceased's needs." [page/13/Text/6], "The present study suggests that most of the fathers may have played the major role in socializing their sons into a stereotypic gender role pattern. In this context, the developmental history of the men in the present study may thus be interpreted as an indication of masculinity in the sense that the deceased were less able to address and handle social defeats, and address negative emotional experiences" [page/14/Text/4], "Our findings related perfectionist tendencies to a history of emotional vulnerability such as shame and humiliation." [page/14/Text/5], "Maladaptive perfectionism among these six men may have originated from shame and humiliation, being the result of unfinished issues/needs for attachment, a desire for autonomy, and an urge to be loved and recognized." [page/14/Text/7]. Recovery: "However, prevention of suicide related to maladaptive perfectionism may basically consist of two strategies: (a) prevent suicide among people who already are maladaptive perfectionists and (b) prevent maladaptive perfectionism among young people. Strategies should include an increased focus upon childrens' upbringing." [page/15/Text/4], "In particular, perfectionistic young people should be encouraged to be more open and be helped to believe in the positive feedback they receive from their supportive social networks, as well as being encouraged to seek professional help if needed. Increasing self-esteem through trust in the self and their own values as opposed to external values is of importance." [page/16/Text/2]
